column5: What are the key challenges (headwinds) and opportunities (tailwinds) impacting growth in your industry? Who are the key competitors?
column6:
Key headwinds:
- Chargeback fraud ("friendly fraud") rising — 60-80% of chargebacks are not real fraud, making evidence quality the deciding factor
- Global chargeback volume projected to exceed $100B annually (LexisNexis Risk Solutions True Cost of Fraud study)
- Stricter issuer policies mean merchants lose more disputes by default
- PCI compliance and multi-system data fragmentation make evidence compilation difficult for small teams

Key tailwinds (industry estimate; consistent across Chargebacks911 and Midigator vendor reports):
- GenAI enables classification, multi-source retrieval, and structured output generation — exactly what chargeback response requires
- Ecommerce platforms (Shopify, WooCommerce) and payment processors (Stripe, Adyen) all have public APIs enabling automated evidence retrieval
- SMB ecommerce growing rapidly — Shopify alone has 1.7M+ merchants globally
- Merchants are increasingly willing to pay SaaS tools for automation (Chargeflow validates $50M ARR)

Projected growth rate: Chargeback management market growing 18-25% CAGR through 2027.

DisputeIQ is a net-new product covering the full chargeback lifecycle across 4 core features:

Feature 1 — Predictive AI for Chargebacks Before Orders Ship:
Flags high-risk orders pre-fulfillment using fraud signals: device risk score, IP/country match, new customer flag, order velocity, AVS/CVV match. MVP uses rules-based scoring with synthetic data. Upgrades to ML model once real platform data flows post-launch. Shown live in the demo opening segment.

Feature 2 — Automated Evidence Aggregation:
Pulls transaction, shipping, customer communication, and platform data across all connected systems automatically. Eliminates 30-45 min of manual copy-paste across 4-6 tools. Platform-agnostic: works with Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, Stripe, PayPal, UPS, FedEx, Zendesk.

Feature 3 — AI Win Probability Prediction:
Scores each dispute with a win likelihood percentage using evidence quality, reason code, customer history. Dashboard shows "72% - Submit" or "18% - Refund instead." Prevents wasted effort on unwinnable disputes.

Feature 4 — Evidence Package Generator:
Generates network-compliant dispute evidence PDFs for Visa and Mastercard submissions. Structured format: transaction summary, proof of authorization, delivery confirmation, customer communication, policy acceptance.

column5: What is the typical journey for your target persona when they are using your product / service, focusing on their ideal experience (happy path) as they interact with your product?
column6:
Current state journey map for Sarah responding to a chargeback:

Step 1 (5 min): Receives chargeback notification via email from Stripe/Shopify — buried in inbox, 7-10 day deadline clock starts immediately

Step 2 (5 min): Opens notification, identifies reason code — codes are cryptic (e.g., "4853 — Cardholder Dispute"), Sarah has to look up what evidence is required

Step 3 (5 min): Logs into Shopify, manually looks up order by transaction ID, screenshots/copies order details

Step 4 (5 min): Logs into UPS/FedEx website separately, enters tracking number, downloads delivery confirmation PDF

Step 5 (5 min): Logs into Zendesk, searches by customer email, screenshots any relevant CSR tickets

Step 6 (10 min): Opens Word template, manually copies data from 3 different systems into formatted PDF

Step 7 (5 min): Logs into chargeback portal (Stripe/Visa), uploads PDF, prays it meets portal-specific requirements

Total: ~40–45 minutes. Repeated 50–200x per month = 25–100 hours of pure manual work monthly.

Emotion: Stressed → frustrated → anxious → drained

column5: Where does the user experience friction, obstacles, or unmet needs throughout the journey? Identify which pain-points are most frequent and severe?
column6:
Pain points ranked by severity:

CRITICAL (AI-solvable):
1. Evidence identification error — Merchants don't know which evidence fields each reason code requires. Missing one field = auto-loss. This is the #1 cause of winnable disputes being lost (20–30% lose winnable cases due to incomplete evidence).

2. Multi-system fragmentation — Evidence lives in 4–6 disconnected systems. No single view. Manual copy-paste is slow and error-prone.

3. Volume overwhelm — At 80 disputes/month, 30 min each = 40 hours. That's essentially one full work week monthly spent only on dispute management.

4. Deadline pressure — 7–10 calendar day window. Multiple deadlines per day for high-volume merchants. Easy to miss.

SECONDARY:
5. Portal-specific formatting — Stripe, Visa, and Mastercard portals have different format requirements (different PDF templates, field names)
6. No win/loss learning — Merchants don't track which evidence strategies win vs. lose, so they repeat the same mistakes

column5:
From your list of pain points, identify those that can effectively be addressed using Generative AI. Remember, this project focuses on leveraging LLM-powered AI to solve your target persona's pain points.

Rank these pain points starting with the most severe and frequently occurring first.
column6:
AI-solvable pain points (where Generative AI adds clear value):

1. Evidence identification (Pain Point #1): LLM + RAG — Feed reason code, retrieve evidence requirements matrix, output exact checklist of required fields. Replaces Sarah needing to know or look up what's required.

2. Multi-source retrieval + synthesis (Pain Point #2): Agentic retrieval — AI calls Shopify, UPS, Zendesk APIs, extracts relevant fields, combines into structured evidence object. Replaces 20 minutes of manual copy-paste.

3. Completeness validation (Pain Point #2): LLM evaluation — AI scores evidence completeness and flags gaps before submission. Reduces "forgot a field" errors.

4. Dispute response document generation (Pain Point #2): LLM structured generation — AI writes professional dispute narrative and formats into portal-specific template. Replaces 10 minutes of manual formatting.

5. Submit vs. Don't Contest recommendation (Pain Point #4): Classification + confidence scoring — AI tells Sarah whether the evidence is strong enough to win, so she doesn't waste time submitting unwinnable cases.

GenAI is particularly well-suited here because: (a) the task is highly structured and repeatable, (b) evidence requirements are rule-based (good for RAG), (c) document generation is a core LLM strength.

column6:
PROMPT A -- Feature 1: Pre-Transaction Risk Scorer (Stage 1)
Covers: Feature 1 only (Predictive AI Before Orders Ship)

---
SYSTEM PROMPT:

You are DisputeIQ's pre-transaction fraud risk analyzer. Your role is to assess whether an incoming order shows signals associated with future chargebacks before the order is fulfilled.

You have expertise in:
- E-commerce fraud patterns (device risk, velocity attacks, friendly fraud indicators)
- Card-not-present fraud signals
- Chargeback risk factors by order type and customer history

When given an order to analyze, you will:
1. Score the order's chargeback risk on a 0-100 scale
2. Identify which specific signals contributed to the score
3. Provide a clear recommendation: PROCEED, FLAG_FOR_REVIEW, or CANCEL

Risk signal weights (rules-based for MVP1, upgrades to ML in MVP2):
- AVS mismatch: +20 points
- IP country does not match billing country: +25 points
- New customer (first order): +10 points
- Order velocity more than 3 orders in 24h from same device: +30 points
- High-value order (over 00) combined with new customer: +15 points
- CVV mismatch: +25 points
- Email domain mismatch with customer name pattern: +10 points

Score thresholds:
- 0-30: LOW RISK -- PROCEED
- 31-60: MEDIUM RISK -- FLAG_FOR_REVIEW
- 61-100: HIGH RISK -- CANCEL or manual verification required

You will receive: order metadata (amount, customer history, device signals, IP data, AVS/CVV results).
You will never receive or process cardholder data (PAN, CVV values, expiry). Order metadata only.

Output format: JSON with fields:
risk_score (0-100), risk_level (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH), signals_triggered (array), recommendation (PROCEED/FLAG_FOR_REVIEW/CANCEL), reasoning (1-2 sentences for merchant display)

IMPORTANT: If a signal field is missing from the input, exclude it from scoring rather than assuming it is a risk. State which signals could not be evaluated.
---

PROMPT B -- Features 2, 3, 4: Dispute Analyst (stage 2)
Covers: Feature 2 (Evidence Aggregation reasoning), Feature 3 (Win Probability Prediction), Feature 4 (Evidence Package Generator)
Note: Feature 2 retrieval is handled by n8n (no AI tokens). Claude receives the pre-assembled evidence bundle and handles classification, scoring, and narrative.

---
SYSTEM PROMPT:

You are DisputeIQ, an expert chargeback analyst AI. Your role is to help e-commerce merchants compile winning chargeback dispute evidence.

You have deep expertise in:
- Visa and Mastercard chargeback reason codes and their evidence requirements
- E-commerce merchant operations (Shopify, Stripe, shipping carriers)
- What constitutes strong vs. weak evidence for each dispute category

When given a chargeback to analyze, you will:
1. Identify the chargeback reason code and explain it in plain English (one sentence)
2. List the specific evidence fields required to win this dispute type
3. Assess what evidence has been retrieved and whether it is sufficient
4. Generate a professional dispute response narrative (150-300 words) in the merchant's voice
5. Output a structured recommendation: SUBMIT, DONT_CONTEST, or REVIEW_MANUALLY with confidence score

You will receive:
- Chargeback metadata (reason code, amount, date)
- Structured evidence object (what was retrieved from each source by n8n)
- Reason code evidence requirements (injected from knowledge base / RAG)

Output format: JSON with fields: reason_code_explanation, required_fields, evidence_assessment, completeness_score, narrative, recommendation, confidence_score, missing_fields

IMPORTANT: You must never hallucinate transaction details. If a piece of evidence is missing, explicitly state it is missing rather than inventing it. A missing evidence declaration is far better than fabricated evidence.

Tone: Professional, factual, merchant-advocate. Write as if preparing a legal brief.
---

column5: What specific quality benchmarks (e.g., clarity, relevance, tone, accuracy, SEO, hallucination avoidance) will define “good” output?
column6:
Quality benchmarks defining a "good" output:

1. Factual accuracy (ZERO tolerance): Every claim in the narrative must be traceable to the input data. No hallucinated dates, amounts, tracking numbers, or names.

2. Completeness accuracy (≥85%): AI correctly identifies which required evidence fields are present, missing, or partial vs. ground truth labels.

3. Recommendation accuracy (≥80%): AI recommendation (SUBMIT/DONT_CONTEST/REVIEW_MANUALLY) matches expert human judgment on 20-case evaluation set.

4. Schema compliance (100%): Output JSON conforms to expected schema — no missing required keys, all values within valid ranges (e.g., confidence_score 0.0–1.0).

5. Narrative quality (≥4/5 human rating): Professional tone, persuasive without overstating evidence, appropriate length (150–300 words), all merchant-specific details accurate.

6. Latency (< 30 seconds end-to-end): From chargeback input received to full output generated.

column5: What specific example use cases, edge cases, and negative cases should be covered by test prompts and outputs?
column6:
20 synthetic test cases across 4 categories:

CATEGORY A — Winnable disputes (10 cases):
• Case 1: "Item Not Received" (13.1) — tracking shows delivered, signature on file → SUBMIT
• Case 2: "Unauthorized Transaction" (10.4) — device fingerprint matches prior orders → SUBMIT
• Case 3: "Item Not as Described" (13.3) — product photos match listing exactly → SUBMIT
• Case 4: "Subscription Cancelled" (13.7) — no cancellation request on file, policy accepted at signup → SUBMIT
• Cases 5–10: Variations of above with high-quality but slightly different evidence

CATEGORY B — Unwinnable disputes (5 cases):
• Case 11: "Item Not Received" — tracking shows returned to sender, never re-delivered → DONT_CONTEST
• Case 12: "Unauthorized Transaction" — device/IP clearly different from all prior orders → DONT_CONTEST
• Case 13: "Item Not as Described" — product clearly different from listing → DONT_CONTEST
• Cases 14–15: Clear legitimate customer complaints

CATEGORY C — Edge cases (5 cases):
• Case 16: Partial tracking — shipped but no delivery scan → REVIEW_MANUALLY
• Case 17: CSR chat shows merchant promised refund but didn't issue one → DONT_CONTEST
• Case 18: Duplicate charge — clearly a processing error → DONT_CONTEST
• Case 19: Subscription cancelled but charged 2 days after → DONT_CONTEST
• Case 20: Missing signature on high-value item — ambiguous → REVIEW_MANUALLY

Each case includes: input data JSON + expected output (recommendation + completeness score range + key evidence fields)

column5: Which AI model is best suited for your solution and why? What capabilities and limitations does it have? How will it integrate with your product?
column6:
Selected model: Anthropic Claude

Primary: Claude Haiku (production — latency and cost optimized at ~$0.25/1M input tokens)
Evaluation/development: Claude Sonnet (prompt iteration and LLM-as-judge evaluation)

Architecture — n8n + Claude split:
- n8n handles workflow orchestration: webhook listeners, API routing, chaining steps between services, retries. Connects to any ecommerce platform and carrier API without burning AI tokens on plumbing.
- Claude Haiku handles AI reasoning only: reason code classification, win probability scoring, evidence assessment, narrative generation. Called only where intelligence is needed.
- RAG: Visa/Mastercard reason code matrix + win prediction rules injected as JSON in system prompt (~5K tokens, no vector DB needed for prototype).
- Frontend: Next.js deployed on Vercel (free tier).
- Claude Code used as the development tool to build and iterate the app.

Why this split matters: Running every workflow step through Claude burns tokens and costs money at scale. n8n does the connecting and routing cheaply, Claude does only the thinking. This is a production-appropriate architecture, not just a prototype choice.

column6:
Required input fields for the AI:

| Field | Format | Source | Notes |
|-------|--------|--------|-------|
| reason_code | String (e.g., "13.1", "4853") | Payment processor notification | Determines entire evidence strategy |
| transaction_id | Alphanumeric string | Payment processor | Links to order in Shopify/Stripe |
| amount | Decimal (USD) | Payment processor | For context and severity assessment |
| transaction_date | ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) | Payment processor | For timeline and deadline calculation |
| merchant_category_code | 4-digit numeric | Merchant profile | Affects applicable network rules |
| order_details | JSON object | Shopify API | Product, price, qty, delivery address |
| tracking_number | String | Shopify/merchant | Required for physical goods disputes |
| delivery_status | Enum (DELIVERED/IN_TRANSIT/RETURNED/FAILED) | Carrier API | Core evidence for Item Not Received |
| delivery_date | ISO 8601 date | Carrier API | Required if DELIVERED |
| customer_service_history | Array of message objects | Zendesk/Intercom API | Required for "Not as Described" |
| tos_acceptance | Object (timestamp + IP) | Merchant database | Required for fraud disputes |

All fields must be present in the structured input JSON passed to the AI model. Missing fields should be passed as null (not omitted) so the AI can explicitly assess them as MISSING.

column5: Are there any optional or user-customizable fields? How do they impact the AI’s output?
column6:
Optional / user-customizable fields:

| Field | Format | Impact on AI Output |
|-------|--------|---------------------|
| customer_signature | Boolean | Strengthens delivery proof for high-value items; adds 10+ pts to completeness score |
| product_photos | Array of image URLs | Required for "not as described" disputes — without this, completeness drops to <50% for that category |
| repeat_customer_flag | Boolean + order_count | Strengthens transaction legitimacy argument in fraud cases |
| device_fingerprint | String | Strengthens fraud defense for "unauthorized transaction" reason codes |
| ip_address_at_purchase | String (IPv4/IPv6) | Supports fraud defense — especially if IP matches customer's billing address location |
| prior_refund_history | Boolean | Indicates if merchant already attempted resolution — changes narrative framing |
| cancellation_policy_url | String (URL) | Required for subscription disputes — without it, policy acceptance claim is weaker |

Note: Some of these fields are "optional" in that the system works without them, but they significantly improve completeness scores and win rates for specific dispute categories.

column5: What criteria will you use to judge output as “good”? (e.g., structure, use of keywords, tone, factuality, relevance)
column6:
Objective criteria for "good" output:

1. Schema compliance (automated): Output JSON must contain all required keys: reason_code_explanation, required_fields, evidence_assessment, completeness_score (0–100), narrative (string), recommendation (SUBMIT/DONT_CONTEST/REVIEW_MANUALLY), confidence_score (0.0–1.0), missing_fields (array)

2. Factual accuracy (automated cross-check): Every factual claim in the narrative must be traceable to a field in the input data. Automated check: extract all dates, amounts, names, addresses from narrative → verify each exists in input JSON.

3. Recommendation accuracy (vs. ground truth): Compare AI recommendation against human expert label on 20-case eval set. Target: ≥80% match.

4. Completeness score calibration: AI completeness score should correlate ≥0.75 (Pearson r) with human expert completeness assessment across eval set.

5. Format compliance: Narrative length 150–300 words (not too terse, not too verbose). All merchant-specific data (name, date, amount) matches input exactly.

column5: Are there any criteria that require human judgment or qualitative assessment?
column6:
Subjective criteria requiring human judgment:

1. Persuasiveness: Would this response be credible to a chargeback analyst at a bank? Does it make a compelling case for the merchant? (1–5 scale, target ≥4)

2. Trust: Would Sarah (ops manager) feel confident submitting this without re-reading the underlying source data? Does the narrative give her confidence that nothing was missed? (1–5 scale, target ≥4)

3. Tone appropriateness: Professional but not overly legalistic. Clear without being condescending. Does not overstate evidence or make promises. (Pass/Fail)

4. Defensibility of recommendation: Is the Submit/Don't Contest recommendation explained well enough that Sarah understands why? If she disagrees, can she easily override with clear rationale? (Pass/Fail)

5. Edge case handling: When evidence is ambiguous, does the AI appropriately flag "Review Manually" rather than confidently recommending Submit on weak evidence? (assessed on edge case subset)

column5: What is your starting system prompt for the model? What variations will you test? What techniques will you use to optimize performance? List initial instructions, persona, inputs, and constraints.
column6:
Prompt Version 1 — Starting system prompt (see Section F27 above for full text).

Key design decisions in v1:
• JSON output format specified explicitly with all field names — reduces schema non-compliance
• Explicit anti-hallucination instruction: "Never hallucinate transaction details. If evidence is missing, declare it missing."
• Tone specification: "Professional, factual, merchant-advocate. Write as if preparing a legal brief."
• Step-by-step output instructions (numbered 1–5) to guide reasoning sequence
• RAG injection: Reason code matrix provided in context per-call

Prompt engineering techniques applied:
• Role assignment ("You are DisputeIQ, an expert chargeback analyst AI")
• Explicit constraints (what NOT to do — no hallucination)
• Output format specification (JSON schema)
• Persona definition (merchant-advocate, professional tone)

Variations to test in iteration:
• v1a: Add few-shot examples showing correct JSON structure
• v1b: Add chain-of-thought instruction ("Before generating recommendation, explicitly reason through each required field")
• v1c: Separate prompts for classification vs. narrative generation (decompose the task)

column5: What examples test the AI’s limits? (e.g., missing data, ambiguous input, out-of-domain)
column6:
Edge cases and negative cases:

EDGE CASE 1 — Partial tracking (shipped but not delivered):
Input: Reason code 13.1, tracking status = "IN_TRANSIT", last scan 5 days ago
Complexity: Package was shipped but no delivery confirmation — ambiguous
Expected output: Recommendation = REVIEW_MANUALLY, Completeness = 55/100
Challenge: AI must resist recommending SUBMIT just because tracking exists

EDGE CASE 2 — CSR chat shows refund promise:
Input: Reason code 4853 (cardholder dispute), Zendesk shows agent told customer "we'll refund you"
Complexity: AI must recognize this as a signal to NOT contest, even if other evidence looks strong
Expected output: Recommendation = DONT_CONTEST, note = "CSR promised refund on [date]"

EDGE CASE 3 — Missing required field for specific reason code:
Input: Reason code 13.3 (not as described), product photos NOT available
Complexity: This dispute category requires product photos — without them, win rate drops sharply
Expected output: Completeness = 45/100, Recommendation = REVIEW_MANUALLY, missing_fields = ["product_photos"]

NEGATIVE CASE 1 — Clear legitimate dispute:
Input: Reason code 10.4 (fraud), device/IP completely different, no prior customer relationship
Expected output: Recommendation = DONT_CONTEST, don't waste time on this

NEGATIVE CASE 2 — Ambiguous input (malformed reason code):
Input: Reason code = null, transaction_id = "ABC123"
Expected output: Error handling — flag for manual review, explain what's missing

column5: Run your input data with the prompt. How did your output perform in manual review? Which examples failed which criteria, and why?
column6:
Manual review results — 3 representative cases tested live against production Vercel deployment (April 2026):

| Case | Scenario | Ground Truth | DisputeIQ Output | Win Probability | Result |
|------|----------|-------------|-----------------|-----------------|--------|
| ORD-44821 | Visa 13.1, DELIVERED, strong evidence | SUBMIT | SUBMIT | 88% | PASS |
| ORD-55902 | Visa 13.1, RETURNED_TO_SENDER | DONT_CONTEST | ABANDON | 8% | PASS |
| ORD-61234 | Visa 10.4, ambiguous fraud signals | REVIEW_MANUALLY | REVIEW | 42% | PASS |

Result: 3/3 cases passed. 100% recommendation accuracy on representative test set.

Hallucination check: Zero hallucinated facts across all three outputs. Every narrative claim traceable to a field in the input evidence bundle. Verified by manual cross-reference of narrative text against input data. Hallucination rate: 0%.

Schema compliance: 100%. All outputs were valid JSON matching the required schema. All required fields present in all outputs.

Latency: Stage 1 approximately 4-6 seconds. stage 2 approximately 8-12 seconds. Both within 30-second target.

Notable failure and fix: In Prompt B v1.0, the win_probability for the REVIEW_MANUALLY case returned 71% — inconsistently high for an ambiguous case. Root cause: scoring logic defaulted optimistic when evidence was partially present. Fix applied in v2.1: added explicit constraint that REVIEW_MANUALLY cases must produce win_probability in the 30-65 range. Post-fix result: 42% (consistent). This is the one documented iteration.

Domain expert validation: Reason code matrix (14 codes) confirmed accurate per Praveena Vichanthangal Prathivathi (Sr Product Manager, Visa), April 2026.

column5: What pass/fail rate or scores did the AI achieve on core criteria?
column6:
Automated evaluation architecture — 5 separate scorers (one per criterion):

| Scorer | Method | Tool | Pass Condition |
|--------|--------|------|----------------|
| Schema compliance | Code check | Python jsonschema validator | Output matches required JSON schema — no missing keys, correct types |
| Hallucination detection | Code check | Cross-reference script: every narrative claim vs. input fields | Zero invented facts |
| Evidence completeness accuracy | LLM-as-judge | Claude Sonnet — single criterion, full input + output + ground truth | Matches expert label |
| Recommendation accuracy | LLM-as-judge | Claude Sonnet — compares recommendation to ground truth | Matches expert label |
| Narrative persuasiveness | LLM-as-judge | Claude Sonnet — "submit without editing" quality bar | Passes quality bar |

Results on 3 tested cases (April 2026):
- Schema compliance: 3/3 PASS (100%)
- Hallucination detection: 3/3 PASS (0% hallucination rate)
- Recommendation accuracy: 3/3 PASS (100% match to ground truth)
- Overall: All tested cases pass all 5 scorer categories

Overall target: 80% or more of 20-case regression set passes all 5 scorers simultaneously.

Test set structure:
- Regression: 20 fixed synthetic cases (eval-cases.md) — run after every prompt change
- Adversarial: 10 break-it-on-purpose inputs — pre-submission to find failure modes
- Post-launch monitoring: 10 real disputes per week once live

Known scorer limitations:
- Length bias: LLM scorers favor longer outputs — narrative scorer calibrated explicitly against concise strong examples
- Same-family bias: Claude scoring Claude output — compensated with Praveena spot-checks as gold standard

column5: What edge cases did you identify in testing or real usage?
column6:
Edge cases identified through design and anticipated from testing:

1. Missing reason code: Chargeback notification PDF doesn't clearly state reason code — AI can't determine evidence requirements
Mitigation: Build reason code parser that extracts from raw text; fallback to "Other" category with general evidence checklist

2. Partial delivery proof: Tracking shows "OUT FOR DELIVERY" but no final scan — evidence exists but incomplete
Mitigation: AI must flag as REVIEW_MANUALLY, not SUBMIT; add explicit constraint in prompt

3. Customer service contradiction: CSR log shows conflicting signals (customer complained but was told issue would be resolved)
Mitigation: AI must summarize CSR history accurately and let human decide — don't auto-recommend based on ambiguous tickets

4. High-value item without signature: Orders over $200 with no signature confirmation — evidence weaker
Mitigation: Flag in completeness assessment: "High-value item — signature confirmation strengthens case significantly"

5. International order: Different shipping carrier, different tracking format — API parsing may fail
Mitigation: Graceful fallback — if carrier API unavailable, mark tracking as MISSING and flag

6. Digital goods dispute: No physical delivery — "Item Not Received" claim on a software download
Mitigation: Detect MCC/product type; switch evidence requirements to digital delivery proof (download logs, activation records)

column5: What prompt or system adjustments have you made based on failures, feedback, or edge case observations?

Prompt updates and adjustments made based on testing (actual — April 2026):

PROMPT A CHANGES (v1.0 to v1.1):
1. Added: Explicit instruction to exclude missing signals from scoring rather than defaulting to zero-risk assumption.
   Reason: v1.0 was ambiguous on how to handle absent fields — led to inconsistent scoring on orders with partial data.

2. Added: Structured signals_triggered array (name + points + description per signal).
   Reason: Frontend display requires per-signal breakdown with explanation. v1.0 returned a flat list.

3. Fixed: email_domain_mismatch weight corrected to +10 (was scoring +25 in v1.0).
   Reason: Model was interpreting the original weight description ambiguously.

PROMPT B CHANGES (v1.0 to v2.1):
1. Added: RAG context injection — 14 Visa/MC reason codes with required evidence fields injected as structured JSON in system context.
   Reason: v1.0 relied on model's training knowledge for reason code requirements. Explicit RAG improves accuracy and consistency.

2. Added: Per-field evidence_assessment structure (status: PRESENT/MISSING/PARTIAL/NOT_REQUIRED + detail per field).
   Reason: Frontend evidence assessment table requires structured per-field data, not a summary.

3. Added: stripe_evidence JSON object — maps DisputeIQ output fields directly to Stripe evidence submission API fields.
   Reason: Enables one-click Stripe submission in production without reformatting.

4. Added: Explicit constraint — if any critical evidence field is MISSING and no compensating evidence exists, recommendation must be DONT_CONTEST or REVIEW_MANUALLY, not SUBMIT.
   Reason: v1.0 produced win_probability 71% on a REVIEW_MANUALLY case. This constraint eliminated the over-confidence issue.

5. Added: Chain-of-thought instruction — assess each evidence field individually before generating recommendation.
   Reason: Improves reasoning transparency and reduces errors on edge cases where evidence is mixed.

column5: What is your chosen approach for evaluation (human, model grader, script)? How will you scale testing to diverse/large test sets?
column6:
Chosen evaluation approach: LLM-as-judge using Claude claude-sonnet-4-6 as evaluator

Why LLM-as-judge:
• 20-case evaluation set is small enough for affordable automated evaluation
• Sonnet can assess narrative quality and persuasiveness better than rule-based scripts
• Allows scaling evaluation beyond what human review bandwidth allows
• Consistent scoring across multiple prompt iterations

Evaluator prompt design:
• Input: DisputeIQ output JSON + original input data + ground truth labels
• Output: Pass/fail on 5 criteria + brief explanation of any failure
• Criteria: (1) Factual accuracy, (2) Completeness accuracy, (3) Recommendation correctness, (4) Narrative quality, (5) Schema compliance

Supplementary approaches:
• Automated script: JSON schema validation (100% coverage, zero human effort)
• Automated script: Hallucination detector (cross-check narrative claims vs. input fields)
• Human spot-check: 5 randomly sampled cases per prompt version reviewed by Praveena (domain expert)

Scaling plan: Once live with real merchant disputes, run weekly automated evaluation on 10 new real cases (with merchant-provided ground truth on outcomes — did they win or lose?)

Privacy framework:
• GDPR (EU merchants): Data deletion on request, data processing agreement available
• PIPEDA (Canadian merchants): Data stored in Canadian AWS region if requested
• CCPA (California merchants): No sale of data; data deletion on request

Security:
• API credentials (Shopify, Stripe) stored encrypted at rest

• P2 — Missing evidence field for a known reason code: Update reason code matrix JSON
• P3 — UI/UX friction or formatting issues: Log in backlog, address in next sprint

ACTION:
• P0/P1: Prompt updated same day, full 20-case eval re-run before re-deployment
• P2: Reason code matrix updated, targeted re-test on affected reason codes
• P3: Logged in GitHub issues, prioritized in next weekly review
• All changes: documented in prompt iteration log (PRD Section F36)

column5: What monitoring/logging is in place to spot operational/AI issues post-launch?
column6:
Monitoring and logging approach:

WORKFLOW LAYER (n8n):
• Native n8n execution logs: every workflow run captured with inputs, outputs, step-by-step results, and error states
• Failed executions: n8n flags and surfaces in dashboard — alerts on consecutive failures
• Retry logic: built into n8n for transient API failures (3 retries with exponential backoff)

AI LAYER (Claude API):
• Token usage logged per call: input tokens, output tokens, latency — tracked to manage cost and detect prompt bloat
• Output schema validation: automated check that every Claude response parses as valid JSON with required keys (reason_code, evidence_items, completeness_score, recommendation, narrative)
• Hallucination sentinel: any evidence_item flagged as "source: inferred" triggers a review queue

FRONTEND (Vercel):
• Vercel Analytics: page load time, error rate, active sessions
• API route error logging: any 5xx from the Next.js API routes logged with request context

THRESHOLDS (post-launch):
• Alert if: JSON parse failure rate >2%, recommendation confidence <50% on >10% of disputes in a day, Claude API latency >5s p95
